abalone.note: The muscular foot, sliced thin against its grain, yields a clean brine and a crunch that softens to velvet — prized raw as sashimi or barely kissed by steam. In Ise and along the Sanriku coast, ama divers have harvested awabi for imperial offerings since ancient times, making it a food that carries the ocean's summer into shrine ceremonies and kaiseki alike.
abalone.peak: Early summer, when currents warm and the sea lettuce blooms

aji-horse-mackerel.note: A silver-skinned fish with a clean, faintly sweet flesh that carries none of the heaviness of fattier blue fish — at its peak now, the meat firms up and develops a bright mineral finish perfect for tataki or sashimi with grated ginger. In the Japanese kitchen, aji announces the shift from spring's delicate flavors toward summer's bolder preparations, often the first fish of the season eaten whole, bones crisped and edible.
aji-horse-mackerel.peak: Early summer through the rainy season, when coastal waters warm

akebi-melon.note: A wild vine fruit with pale lavender skin that cracks to reveal translucent, seed-studded flesh tasting faintly of honeydew and lychee — the soft interior is eaten fresh while the bitter rind is stuffed with miso-seasoned meat and fried. Gathered from mountain forests rather than cultivated, akebi marks the season when foragers turn their attention from summer abundance to autumn's quieter, harder-won gifts.
akebi-melon.peak: Early autumn, when the mountain air turns crisp and the fruit splits open of its own accord

amanatsu.note: A thick-skinned hybrid citrus whose flesh delivers bright acidity tempered by a honeyed undertone, the bitterness of its pith prized for marmalades and candied peel. Harvested in winter but left to cure until the warmth arrives, amanatsu bridges the citrus season's end with the first humid days of early summer.
amanatsu.peak: Late spring through early summer, when the citrus has mellowed on the branch

amanatsu-citrus.note: Harvested in winter but left to mellow until April or May, amanatsu trades sharpness for a honeyed acidity, its thick pith still carrying enough pleasant bitterness to wake the palate. This is the citrus that bridges the gap between cold-weather mikan and summer's arrival, appearing in marmalades and refreshing desserts just as the air turns humid.
amanatsu-citrus.peak: Late spring into early summer, when the skin finally yields its bitterness

amanatsu-sweet-citrus.note: A thick-skinned citrus whose flesh balances bright acidity with a honeyed sweetness that only emerges after months of patient storage past the winter harvest. The segments are often eaten fresh with a small fork at the breakfast table, or candied into marmalade that catches the last of spring's light.
amanatsu-sweet-citrus.peak: Late spring through early summer, when the bitter edge of winter citrus has mellowed

anago-conger-eel.note: Unlike its richer cousin unagi, anago offers a delicate, almost ephemeral sweetness, its pale flesh turning silky when simmered in a light soy broth or brushed with nikiri and torched atop sushi. It appears as the humidity thickens, a gentle protein that suits the season's call for foods that nourish without weighing heavy on the body.
anago-conger-eel.peak: Early summer through the rainy season, when the flesh reaches its sweetest

aoyuzu-green-yuzu.note: Harvested unripe, green yuzu offers a sharper, more herbaceous bite than its mature form — the zest bright with volatile oils that sting the nose pleasantly when grated over warm dishes. It appears in kitchens just as summer's humidity begins to break, its astringent perfume cutting through rich grilled fish and lending an edge to ponzu made for the cooling months ahead.
aoyuzu-green-yuzu.peak: Late summer through early autumn, before the fruit turns gold

ashitaba.note: A coastal herb from the Izu Islands whose thick stems weep golden sap when cut — the flavor sits between celery and angelica, with a faint medicinal bitterness that tempura transforms into something almost sweet. Its name means 'tomorrow's leaf,' a promise kept each morning as harvested stalks push out new growth overnight, embodying the quiet persistence that Japanese cooks honor in their spring greens.
ashitaba.peak: Late spring through early summer, when the stems are still tender and the sap runs yellow

ayu-sweetfish.note: A slender river fish whose flesh carries the faint fragrance of watermelon and fresh cucumber—the result of feeding on algae from clean mountain streams. Salt-grilled whole on skewers, its bitter entrails prized, ayu announces the arrival of summer and the opening of cormorant fishing season along the Nagara River.
ayu-sweetfish.peak: Early summer through mid-autumn, when rivers run cool and clear

bamboo-shoots.note: Dug at dawn before the sun can turn their sugars bitter, fresh takenoko have a faint sweetness and a texture that yields with a clean snap — nothing like the pallid canned version. Their arrival marks the brief window when the kitchen turns to wakegi and sansho leaves, dishes assembled quickly to honor what will not wait.
bamboo-shoots.peak: Late spring, from the grain rains through the first whispers of summer

bamboo-shoots-takenoko.note: Freshly dug takenoko must reach the pot within hours, before its sugars turn to woody bitterness; the flesh should taste faintly sweet, with a clean vegetal snap unlike anything that has traveled far. Its arrival marks the threshold when winter's preserved foods give way to the brief, urgent harvests of spring.
bamboo-shoots-takenoko.peak: Late spring, during kokuu — the grain rains that coax pale tips through dark soil

beltfish.note: Named for its resemblance to a Japanese sword, the tachiuo is a ribbon of silver that swims vertically in deep waters, its flesh turning translucent and sweet as autumn deepens. Grilled with salt until the skin blisters and chars, it arrives at tables just as the nights grow long enough to warrant a second cup of sake.
beltfish.peak: Late summer through autumn, when the fish fatten before winter's cold

bitter-melon.note: The warted jade skin yields to a spongy, pale interior whose bracing bitterness cuts through the humidity like a cold cloth on the neck. In Okinawa, it anchors the iconic gōyā champurū, a stir-fry that has carried islanders through centuries of subtropical summers.
bitter-melon.peak: High summer, when the cicadas reach their full chorus

bitter-melon-g-ya.note: This ridged, warty gourd yields flesh of startling bitterness — a quality prized precisely because it cools the body and sharpens the appetite when humid air sits heavy on the skin. In Okinawa, where it climbs trellises against the brutal sun, gōya champurū with tofu and egg remains the essential dish for surviving the long days of taisho, the great heat.
bitter-melon-g-ya.peak: High summer, when the heat grows thick and unrelenting

biwa-loquat.note: Beneath thin, tawny skin lies flesh the color of pale apricot, yielding and faintly perfumed, with a sweetness that recalls honey warmed by afternoon sun. The biwa arrives in those fleeting weeks between spring's end and summer's humidity, its season so brief that eating one becomes an act of attention to time itself.
biwa-loquat.peak: Late spring to early summer, when the plum rains have not yet arrived

biwa-loquat-early.note: These early loquats arrive with skin still pale orange and flesh that yields a bright, faintly tart sweetness — not yet the honeyed depth of peak season, but refreshing as a first sip of something cold. The biwa's brief window marks the threshold between spring's last coolness and the approaching weight of tsuyu, the plum rains.
biwa-loquat-early.peak: Late spring into early summer, when the first warm rains give way to humid days

blueberry.note: Japanese blueberries grown in highland orchards reach their sweetest point in July and August, their skins taut with a bloom of pale dust that smudges at the touch. Eaten chilled from the refrigerator or folded into yogurt, they mark the brief window when summer fruit can still refresh rather than cloy.
blueberry.peak: High summer, when the cicadas reach their fullest chorus

bonito.note: The first bonito of the season, called hatsugatsuo, arrives lean and clean-fleshed, its deep red meat best eaten as tataki — seared over straw fire until the edges char while the center stays cool and raw. In Edo times, people paid small fortunes for the year's first catch, believing it added seventy-five days to one's life.
bonito.peak: Late spring into early summer, when the kuroshio current carries them northward

bonito-katsuo.note: The spring bonito, called hatsu-gatsuo, runs lean and firm with a clean, almost metallic brightness that sashimi lovers prize for its lack of fattiness. This 'first bonito' has been celebrated since the Edo period as a harbinger of summer, when merchants would pay a fortune for the season's inaugural catch, believing it added years to one's life.
bonito-katsuo.peak: Late spring through early summer, when the first catch arrives with the warm Kuroshio Current

bud-japanese-grapes.note: Japanese grapes like Kyoho and Shine Muscat are prized for flesh that slips clean from the skin, intensely sweet with a musky depth that fills the mouth. They arrive as Obon offerings fade and moon-viewing season approaches, their dark clusters echoing the deepening nights.
bud-japanese-grapes.peak: Late summer through early autumn, when the air turns crisp and vine leaves begin to bronze

cherry.note: Japanese cherries arrive with flesh so tender it yields at the slightest pressure, their sweetness balanced by a faint tartness that lingers on the tongue. The brief harvest marks a fleeting pause between spring's blossoms and summer's full heat — a fruit enjoyed quickly, often simply, before its moment passes.
cherry.peak: Early summer, when the rainy season's first mists settle over the orchards

conger-eel.note: Anago offers a gentler, more delicate sweetness than its cousin unagi — its flesh turning silken when brushed with sweet soy and kissed by charcoal flame. The eel emerges from sandy burrows as waters warm, arriving on sushi counters and in fluffy egg custards just as summer settles into its humid pulse.
conger-eel.peak: Early summer through mid-autumn, when the flesh carries its sweetest fat

conger-eel-anago.note: Unlike its richer cousin unagi, anago offers a lighter, more delicate sweetness — its pale flesh turns silken when simmered in sweet soy, draped warm over sushi rice in Edomae style. The eel fattens as waters warm toward tsuyu, making it a gentle bridge between spring's clarity and summer's abundance.
conger-eel-anago.peak: Early summer through the rainy season, when the flesh reaches its sweetest

cucumber.note: Sliced thin and dressed with nothing more than salt and rice vinegar, the summer cucumber offers a clean snap and faint grassy sweetness that cuts through the weight of humid days. It appears in sunomono, pressed into nukazuke pickles overnight, or simply eaten whole with a dab of miso — the edible equivalent of a cold washcloth pressed to the nape of the neck.
cucumber.peak: Early summer through the humid months, when the body craves what is cool and crisp

early-cherries.note: These earliest cherries arrive with flesh still firm and flavor caught between sweet and tart — a brightness that speaks of orchards not yet heavy with full summer. In Japan, they mark the brief window after cherry blossoms fall and before the plum rains begin, eaten chilled from the hand as a fleeting luxury.
early-cherries.peak: Late spring through early summer, as the first warm rains give way to longer days

early-harvest-persimmon-kaki.note: These early-harvest persimmons arrive while still carrying a faint astringency, their flesh firm enough to slice cleanly, revealing that particular orange that seems to hold the last warmth of summer. In the Japanese kitchen, they mark the pivot from summer's watery fruits to autumn's denser sweetness — eaten fresh with a sprinkle of salt, or dried on farmhouse eaves as the days shorten.
early-harvest-persimmon-kaki.peak: Early autumn, when the first cool nights deepen the fruit's color

early-peach.note: The first peaches of the season arrive smaller and firmer than their midsummer kin, their flesh yielding a clean, almost floral sweetness that carries a whisper of tartness near the stone. In the Japanese kitchen, these early fruits are often eaten chilled and unadorned, a brief pleasure marking the threshold between rainy season and the fierce light of true summer.
early-peach.peak: Late June through early July, as the plum rains taper and summer heat begins to press

early-pear.note: These first nashi of the season arrive with flesh so crisp it shatters against the teeth, their juice running clear and faintly honeyed before the deeper sweetness of later harvests develops. In the humid weight of lingering summer, their clean, quenching bite signals the quiet turn toward autumn's relief.
early-pear.peak: Late summer into early autumn, when the first cool nights arrive

edamame.note: Young soybeans harvested still clinging to the branch, their pods furred with fine hairs that hold the morning dew; bite through and the beans slide out with a faint sweetness, tasting of green growth and salt. They arrive with the beer-drinking season, piled in wooden bowls at summer festivals and on verandas where evenings finally cool.
edamame.peak: High summer, when cicadas reach full chorus

fava-beans.note: Called 'sky beans' for the way their pods point upward on the stem, these legumes arrive with a fleeting sweetness and grass-green fragrance that disappears within days of harvest. Grilled whole in their woolly pods until charred, or simply boiled with coarse salt, they mark the narrow window between cherry blossoms and the arrival of tsuyu rains.
fava-beans.peak: Late spring, when pods turn skyward before the humid season

fava-beans-soramame.note: Named 'sky beans' for the way their pods point upward before harvest, soramame offer a fleeting sweetness best captured within three days of picking — grilled in their pods until charred, the beans inside turn creamy with a faint grassy brightness. Their arrival marks the threshold between spring's gentle cool and early summer's humidity, a moment when Japanese cooks race against time to preserve this brief, verdant window.
fava-beans-soramame.peak: Late spring, when pods swell skyward in the warming sun

fig-ichijiku.note: The flesh yields to the teeth in a way that feels almost liquid — honey-sweet with a faint graininess from the countless tiny seeds within. Eaten fresh at breakfast or simmered into preserves, the fig marks the season's turn, arriving just as summer's intensity starts to soften.
fig-ichijiku.peak: Late summer through early autumn, when the air begins to cool

flounder.note: A flatfish whose paper-thin sashimi reveals an almost translucent sweetness, the meat gaining density and fat as winter deepens. In the Japanese kitchen, karei appears as engawa—the prized fin-edge muscle—or simmered whole in soy and ginger, a dish that speaks of shortened days and the patience of slow cooking.
flounder.peak: Late autumn through winter, when cold currents firm the flesh

fuki-butterbur.note: Pale green stems with a mineral bitterness that lingers clean on the tongue, their hollow centers ideal for simmering in dashi until the fibers turn silken. After the fleeting fuki-no-tō buds of early spring, these mature stalks arrive as the season's quieter second act — peeled, blanched, and often preserved as tsukudani to carry spring's memory into the humid months ahead.
fuki-butterbur.peak: Late spring, when the stalks reach full height before summer's weight

ginkgo-nuts.note: Beneath their notoriously pungent flesh, these jade-green kernels offer a texture between chestnut and edamame, with a faint bitterness that deepens when skewered and salt-grilled over charcoal. Threaded onto pine needles in kaiseki courses or scattered through chawanmushi, they mark the turning toward winter with their almost resinous warmth.
ginkgo-nuts.peak: Late autumn, when the first hard frosts sweeten the fallen seeds

grape.note: Japanese grapes arrive heavy on the stem, their skins slipping free to reveal flesh so sweet it borders on floral — varieties like Kyoho and Shine Muscat prized for size, fragrance, and that first cold bite. They mark the turning season, appearing on altars for Obon and lingering through the harvest moon, a fruit eaten slowly, one globe at a time.
grape.peak: Late summer through early autumn, when nights begin to cool and sugars concentrate in the flesh

green-peas.note: Freshly shelled peas possess a sweetness that fades within hours of harvest — their sugars converting to starch even as you carry them home. In the Japanese kitchen, they arrive just as rice fields flood for planting, their vivid green scattered over bamboo-basket lunches or folded into mame-gohan, marking the brief window before summer's heat.
green-peas.peak: Late spring, when the pods swell plump between the rains

green-pepper.note: Summer-harvested specimens have thin, yielding walls and a clean vegetal bitterness that children famously protest and adults come to crave — char them quickly over high flame until the skin blisters and the flesh turns silken. In the humid depths of July, they appear sliced into glistening stir-fries with jako sardines, or stuffed with pork and glazed in sweet soy, humble dishes that speak to the season's need for dishes both quick and restorative.
green-pepper.peak: Early summer through late August, when the heat draws out their grassy brightness

green-shiso.note: The jagged leaves release their unmistakable fragrance only when torn or bruised — a sharp, almost mentholated freshness that cuts through the heaviness of raw fish and summer heat. In the old kitchen calendar, shiso marks the season when food spoils quickly; its natural antimicrobial oils made it the cook's quiet ally against decay.
green-shiso.peak: Early summer through the humid months, when leaves grow lush before flowering

green-shiso-ba.note: These broad, serrated leaves release a bright, almost electric fragrance when torn — part mint, part basil, part something wilder that belongs only to itself. In the sweltering kitchen of high summer, a single leaf laid beneath sashimi or floated in cold sōmen broth cuts through the heat with its clean, camphoraceous edge.
green-shiso-ba.peak: Early summer through the humid months, when its oils are most fragrant

green-ume-plums.note: Hard, astringent, and intensely fragrant, green plums arrive too sour to eat raw — their purpose is transformation. Soaked in shochu with rock sugar, they become umeshu by winter; packed in salt, they yield the umeboshi that will see a household through the year.
green-ume-plums.peak: Early summer, as the rains begin to veil the mountains

grunt.note: The striped beakfish, called ishidai for its habit of crushing shellfish against stones, yields firm white flesh with a clean mineral sweetness prized in sashimi and usuzukuri. Its arrival at market signals the transition from spring's delicate flavors toward summer's more robust catch, a threshold fish served at gatherings marking the season's turn.
grunt.peak: Late spring through early summer, as waters warm along rocky coastlines

hamo.note: A serpentine eel with flesh so riddled with fine bones that only practiced knife-work—hundreds of cuts per fillet—renders it edible, the blade releasing a texture both silken and faintly resilient. In landlocked Kyoto, hamo arrived alive in buckets of seawater from Osaka Bay, becoming the essential luxury of summer: served as tempura, in clear broth, or blanched until its scored flesh blooms white like chrysanthemum petals.
hamo.peak: High summer, when Kyoto's Gion Festival lanterns sway in the humid air

hamo-pike-conger.note: A serpentine eel prized in Kyoto despite the sea being hours away — its flesh stays firm in summer heat, and skilled knife work transforms hundreds of hairline bones into something that blooms like a white flower when blanched. Essential to Gion Festival cuisine in July, where it arrives as hamo-otoshi: slices shocked in ice water, served with tart umeboshi paste to cut the humid air.
hamo-pike-conger.peak: Rainy season through midsummer, when the flesh grows richest before spawning

horse-mackerel.note: A silvery fish with a distinctive lateral line of bony scutes, its flesh now carries the clean, faintly sweet fat that comes before the humid months — best eaten as tataki, seared just at the edges, or in sashimi so fresh the meat still has tension. In fishing villages, aji signals the turn toward summer's abundance, its arrival at market coinciding with the first hydrangeas.
horse-mackerel.peak: Early summer through the rainy season, when coastal waters warm

horse-mackerel-aji.note: A silver-sided fish with a distinctive row of bony scutes along its lateral line, aji at its peak carries a clean sweetness and firm flesh that needs nothing more than a squeeze of ginger and scallion as tataki or namero. It arrives as the hydrangeas bloom and the rainy season lifts, a bright counterpoint to the heaviness of tsuyu.
horse-mackerel-aji.peak: Early summer through midsummer, when coastal waters warm and schools run fat

hotaru-ika-firefly-squid.note: These thumb-sized squid rise from deep waters to spawn, their photophores glowing an ethereal blue-white—eaten whole, their bodies burst with a briny sweetness and faint bitterness from the viscera. In Toyama, the arrival of hotaru ika announces spring's true arrival, boiled simply in salted water or dressed in vinegared miso, a fleeting delicacy gone by May.
hotaru-ika-firefly-squid.peak: Late spring, when night tides carry blue phosphorescence into Toyama Bay

ichigo-strawberries.note: Japanese strawberries are bred for sweetness over tartness, their flesh yielding and fragrant, often eaten unadorned or perched atop shortcake in pristine rows. Though available year-round now, their true season arrives with the cold months, when varieties like Amaou and Tochiotome appear as gifts and symbols of celebration, their red brightness a quiet herald that spring will follow.
ichigo-strawberries.peak: Late winter through spring, when greenhouse cultivation meets rising warmth

isaki-grunt.note: A handsome striped fish whose flesh reaches its richest state just before spawning — firm yet yielding, with a clean sweetness that needs only salt and flame. Grilled whole over charcoal, its skin blistering and fat dripping, isaki signals the threshold between spring's delicacy and summer's abundance.
isaki-grunt.peak: Early summer, when hydrangeas begin to color the hillsides

ishidai-striped-beakfish.note: A powerful reef fish with a parrot-like beak and bold black stripes that fade with age, its firm white flesh carries a clean, faintly sweet taste prized for sashimi — the texture dense enough to resist the teeth before yielding. Considered the king of rock-dwelling fish among anglers, ishidai arrives at its fattest in early summer when it feeds voraciously before spawning, marking the season when serious fishermen test their skill against its legendary strength.
ishidai-striped-beakfish.peak: Early summer, as waters warm along rocky coastlines

iwashi-sardine.note: The silvery skin flashes blue-green like oil on water, and the meat beneath runs dark and rich with the fat that will carry the fish through lean months. Grilled over charcoal until the skin blisters and chars, or simmered with ginger and soy until the bones soften to nothing, iwashi arrives at the table smelling of the sea and woodsmoke — humble fare that nonetheless marks the turning toward winter's depths.
iwashi-sardine.peak: Late autumn through winter, when cold currents fatten the flesh

j-roku-sasage-yard-long-beans.note: Named for the sixteen seeds that line each slender pod, these beans snap with a grassy sweetness and cook to a silken texture that green beans cannot match. In the Obon season, they appear in shōjin ryōri offerings and simple ohitashi, their deep green a quiet counterpoint to the summer's relentless brightness.
j-roku-sasage-yard-long-beans.peak: High summer, when the cicadas reach full chorus

japanese-pear.note: Unlike Western pears, nashi yields a crisp, granular flesh that shatters between the teeth, its juice cool and faintly floral — chilled slices served after dinner carry the first relief of cooler nights. The arrival of nashi marks the true pivot from summer's heaviness, appearing on offering trays during Obon and remaining through the harvest moon viewing of mid-autumn.
japanese-pear.peak: Early autumn, when cicada song gives way to cricket chirp

japanese-pear-nashi.note: Unlike its Western cousins, nashi offers a crisp, granular flesh that shatters between the teeth with a spray of cool, faintly floral juice — refreshment distilled into fruit form. Chilled slices appear at summer's end as a gesture of hospitality, their pale sweetness marking the pivot from lingering heat toward the clear skies of autumn.
japanese-pear-nashi.peak: Late summer through early autumn, when cicada song begins to fade

japanese-plum.note: These small stone fruits arrive with flesh that ranges from honey-gold to deep crimson, their skin taut and faintly dusty, yielding to a sweetness edged with bright acidity. They appear just as the rainy season lifts, a fleeting bridge between the heaviness of tsuyu and the blazing days of true summer.
japanese-plum.peak: Early summer through mid-summer, when cicadas first test their voices

kabocha-squash.note: A dense-fleshed winter squash with deep green rind and flesh the color of persimmon, prized for its chestnut-like sweetness that intensifies in storage. Eaten on the winter solstice to ward off colds, its golden flesh brings the memory of autumn sun to the darkest tables of the year.
kabocha-squash.peak: Late autumn through winter solstice, when the flesh sweetens after the first frost

kabocha-winter-squash.note: A dense-fleshed winter squash with dry, chestnut-like sweetness and skin tender enough to eat — the flesh turns almost jam-thick when simmered in dashi and soy. Central to the winter solstice meal called tōji, when eating kabocha is believed to ward off colds and carry one safely through the darkest nights.
kabocha-winter-squash.peak: Late autumn through winter solstice, when frost has concentrated the sugars

kabosu-citrus.note: A golf ball-sized citrus from Ōita Prefecture, kabosu yields a juice more rounded than sudachi, less bitter than lemon — its pale green flesh releasing an aroma somewhere between bergamot and fresh-cut grass when squeezed over grilled sanma. As the first mackerel pike of autumn arrives, so too does kabosu reach the table, the two inseparable in the September kitchen.
kabosu-citrus.peak: Late summer through early autumn, when the green rind holds its sharpest fragrance

kawahagi-filefish.note: The lean white flesh is almost transparent, mild to the point of sweetness, but it is the liver — creamy, rich as foie gras, tinged faintly orange — that devotees prize, mashed into soy sauce as a dipping medium for the sashimi. As autumn turns and the filefish fattens its liver against winter, sushi counters in Tokyo quietly shift their attention from summer's light catches to this homely fish with its sandpaper skin.
kawahagi-filefish.peak: Late autumn into early winter, when the liver swells with fat before the deep cold

kisu-japanese-whiting.note: A slender, silver-skinned fish whose flesh is so delicate and clean-tasting it seems to dissolve on the tongue — the definitive tempura fish, its light sweetness heightened by a whisper-thin batter. Kisu appears as beach-going season begins, caught by surf fishermen standing knee-deep in the shallows, marking the transition from spring's heavier flavors to summer's crystalline simplicity.
kisu-japanese-whiting.peak: Early summer through late autumn, when shallow waters warm along sandy shores

kisu-sillago.note: A slender, silver-skinned fish with flesh so delicate and clean it seems to hold the lightness of early summer itself — the classic tempura-dane, its fillets curling golden in the oil while staying sweet and faintly briny within. Kisu signals the true arrival of the season for coastal pleasures, appearing on menus just as families begin to think of ocean breezes and salt air.
kisu-sillago.peak: Early summer, when beach waters warm and the fish draw near the shallows

kisu-whiting.note: A slender silver fish with flesh so delicate it seems to dissolve on the tongue, prized for tempura where its clean sweetness emerges through the lightest batter. Kisu announces the arrival of summer along sandy shorelines, its presence in the kitchen marking the shift from spring's heavier broths to the season of crisp, oil-kissed simplicity.
kisu-whiting.peak: Early summer, when coastal waters warm and fishing boats return with the first light

kohada-gizzard-shad.note: A slender silver fish whose skin shimmers with an iridescent blue-green sheen, kohada is prized for its delicate balance of rich oils and clean brine — the vinegar cure of edomae sushi tradition draws out its brightness without masking the sea. As winter deepens, the fish grows from shinko to kohada to konoshiro, each stage a fleeting window the sushi shokunin watches for with the patience of reading tides.
kohada-gizzard-shad.peak: Late autumn through winter, when cold waters tighten the flesh

kuruma-ebi-japanese-tiger-prawn.note: Named for the striped wheel-like pattern that curves along its shell, this prawn offers flesh that is sweet, firm, and faintly translucent — prized raw as odori, still quivering, or graced by the lightest tempura batter. It marks the season when edomae sushi reaches its quiet peak, the prawn poached just so, brushed with sweet soy, and pressed warm against seasoned rice.
kuruma-ebi-japanese-tiger-prawn.peak: Early summer through autumn, when waters warm along the Inland Sea

ky-ri-cucumber.note: Japanese cucumbers arrive slender and thin-skinned, their flesh dense with a grassy sweetness that shatters cleanly between the teeth — nothing like their waterlogged Western cousins. Salted and pressed into asazuke, or simply split and dipped in miso, they offer the kitchen its first true relief from summer's gathering heat.
ky-ri-cucumber.peak: Early summer through the humid height of tsuyu, when morning harvests carry the cool of night

kyoho-grape.note: These dark purple grapes slip from their skins with a gentle squeeze, revealing translucent flesh so sweet and musky it perfumes the fingers. Their arrival signals the threshold between summer's end and autumn's gathering, when fruit bowls shift from bright citrus to the deeper, wine-dark tones of the cooling season.
kyoho-grape.peak: Late summer through early autumn, when cicada songs begin to fade

late-strawberries.note: These final strawberries of the season arrive smaller and deeply flushed, their sugars concentrated by warming days into an almost jammy intensity that the pale spring berries never achieve. Japanese cooks prize them for preserves and strawberry daifuku, capturing the fruit's fleeting sweetness just before the fields go quiet until winter forcing begins again.
late-strawberries.peak: Early summer, as the first hydrangeas begin to color

loquat.note: Beneath its thin, downy skin lies flesh the color of apricot preserve — yielding, faintly tart, with a floral sweetness that vanishes almost as quickly as it arrives. The loquat's brief season bridges the gap between cherry blossoms and the first summer fruits, its clusters of golden orbs a quiet signal that the rains will soon come.
loquat.peak: Late spring to early summer, when the hydrangeas begin to bud

loquats-biwa.note: Beneath thin, suede-like skin lies flesh the color of apricot sunset — faintly tart, honeyed, with a floral finish that dissolves on the tongue. The loquat arrives just as spring exhausts itself, a brief sweetness before the plum rains settle in.
loquats-biwa.peak: Early summer, when hydrangeas begin to blur with color

lotus-root.note: Cut crosswise, the wheel reveals its lace of air pockets — a pattern read as 'seeing clearly into the future,' making it essential to New Year's osechi. Simmered in nimono it turns silken and faintly sweet; sliced thin and fried, it shatters between the teeth like autumn frost.
lotus-root.peak: Late autumn through winter, when cold sharpens the starches

m-i-cucumber-okinawan-cucumber.note: A pale, thick-skinned heirloom cucumber from Okinawa with crisp, almost melon-like flesh that stays cool and firm even in brutal subtropical heat. Sliced thin and dressed with a whisper of vinegar or simmered gently in awamori-spiked broth, it carries the quiet endurance of Ryukyuan summers to the table.
m-i-cucumber-okinawan-cucumber.peak: Early summer through typhoon season, when Okinawan sun is most relentless

maitake-hen-of-the-woods-mushroom.note: Found clustered at the base of old oaks and chestnuts, maitake unfolds in rippling bronze-gray fronds with an earthy fragrance and a texture that stays toothsome whether grilled with a brush of soy or torn into tempura batter. Its name — 'dancing mushroom' — recalls the joy of foragers who once danced upon discovering these elusive clusters, a sign that the mountain's larder had opened for the cooling season.
maitake-hen-of-the-woods-mushroom.peak: Early to mid-autumn, when the first cold nights settle into the mountain forests

manganji-pepper.note: A long, thick-fleshed sweet pepper from Maizuru, Kyoto — virtually without heat, its skin blisters and chars beautifully over flame, releasing a green sweetness that tastes of summer rain on warm soil. Grilled whole and dressed with nothing but soy and bonito, it embodies the elegant restraint of Kyoto's vegetable tradition, the kyō-yasai that define the old capital's table.
manganji-pepper.peak: Early summer through late August, when Kyoto's fields are heavy with heat

manganji-peppers.note: These long, slender peppers from Maizuru carry almost no heat — just a grassy sweetness and skin so thin it blisters in seconds over high flame, releasing a faint char perfume. Kyoto cooks prize them simply grilled with a brush of soy, their arrival marking the shift from spring's delicacy to summer's bold, direct flavors.
manganji-peppers.peak: Early summer through midsummer, when Kyoto's basin heat coaxes their sweetness

mango.note: Miyazaki's Taiyo no Tamago mangoes arrive with flesh so dense and perfumed it yields like custard beneath the knife, their skin blushing from green to sunset red. They mark the apex of summer gift-giving season, wrapped in protective nets and presented in paulownia boxes as offerings of gratitude during ochūgen.
mango.peak: High summer, from the solstice through the cicada chorus of late July

mango-okinawan.note: Okinawan mangoes, predominantly the Irwin variety, are harvested only after they drop naturally into nets suspended beneath the trees — their flesh a deep saffron, almost custardy, with a fragrance that fills a room before the knife touches skin. They arrive as mainland Japan enters its most oppressive heat, a gift from the southern islands that transforms the season's discomfort into fleeting sweetness.
mango-okinawan.peak: High summer, when Okinawa's subtropical sun reaches its zenith

matsutake-mushrooms.note: Emerging from the duff beneath aged red pines, matsutake releases a scent both spicy and resinous — somewhere between cinnamon bark and wet stone — that no other mushroom possesses. Its arrival marks the threshold of autumn's deepest turn, celebrated in dobinmushi, where the fragrance rises with the steam from a lidded teapot, carrying the forest to the table.
matsutake-mushrooms.peak: Early to mid-autumn, when the first cold rains settle into red pine forests

mikan-late-variety.note: These late-ripening satsuma mandarins have thicker skins and denser flesh than their autumn cousins, their sweetness deepened by months of winter chill into something almost honeyed. They appear in kotatsu-warmed rooms as the year turns, the last bright notes of citrus before spring's first strawberries arrive.
mikan-late-variety.peak: Late winter through early spring, when cold has concentrated the sugars

mitsuba.note: Three-lobed leaves on hollow stems carry a fragrance somewhere between celery and angelica, bright and faintly peppery, releasing their scent the moment they meet hot broth. A finishing herb rather than a cooked one, mitsuba floats atop chawanmushi and clear soups at the threshold of the new year, its pale green a quiet signal that warmth is returning.
mitsuba.peak: Early spring, when snow-melt still lingers in mountain valleys

molokhia.note: An Egyptian mallow whose dark, almost jade leaves release a silken mucilage when chopped, thickening soups with a vegetal richness that clings to the spoon. In Japan it arrives as a cooling counterpoint to the humid weight of late July, often minced raw with soy and served over cold rice when appetite wavers in the heat.
molokhia.peak: High summer, when the cicadas reach their fullest chorus

momo-early-peaches.note: These early peaches arrive with flesh still pale and firm, their sweetness restrained, carrying a faint astringency that softens only after a day on the kitchen counter. They mark the threshold of summer's true abundance, appearing just as the rainy season lifts and the land turns toward ripening.
momo-early-peaches.peak: Early summer, as the first heat settles into the valleys

momo-white-peach.note: The white peach yields to the slightest pressure, its flesh so delicate it bruises at a glance — the juice runs clear and fragrant, tasting of flowers more than fruit. In Japan, a perfect momo arrives swaddled in foam netting like something precious, offered as a summer gift when words alone feel insufficient.
momo-white-peach.peak: High summer, from late July through August when the heat draws out the sugars

muscat-grape.note: Shine Muscat grapes arrive with skins so thin you eat them whole, their flesh crisp and perfumed with a sweetness that tastes almost of white flowers. They mark the pivot from summer's heaviness toward autumn's clarity, arranged in lacquered boxes as gifts during the season of gratitude.
muscat-grape.peak: Late summer through early autumn, when the nights begin to cool

muscat-grapes.note: Japanese Shine Muscat grapes yield to the teeth with a crisp snap, their translucent jade flesh releasing a perfume somewhere between lychee and white flowers — eaten skin and all, no seeds to interrupt the pleasure. They arrive as Obon visits end and children return to school, a jeweled sweetness marking the turn toward cooler days.
muscat-grapes.peak: Early autumn, when summer's heat finally loosens its grip

my-ga.note: These pale pink buds emerge from the soil with a sharp, clean fragrance — sliced thin, they cut through the heaviness of summer with their peppery bite and subtle resin. Scattered raw over chilled sōmen or pickled in sweet vinegar, myōga arrives just as the body craves something bracing before the long exhale of autumn.
my-ga.peak: Late summer into early autumn, when humidity still hangs in the air

my-ga-ginger-bud.note: The pale pink bud of a wild ginger relative, sliced into threads that release a clean, resinous bite — bright against cold sōmen or scattered over chilled tofu. Its fleeting pungency belongs to the humid days when appetite falters and the body craves something sharp to cut through the weight of August.
my-ga-ginger-bud.peak: High summer through early autumn, when the buds push through damp shade

my-ga-ginger-buds.note: These pale pink torpedo-shaped buds carry a bright, resinous sting that cuts through the heaviness of humid days — sliced thin, they shatter against cold sōmen or float in clear soup. In the old kitchen calendar, myōga signals the turn toward lighter eating, a small sharp awakening when the body craves nothing rich.
my-ga-ginger-buds.peak: High summer through early autumn, when the buds push through damp shade

my-ga-ginger-shoots.note: These torpedo-shaped flower buds carry a bright, resinous bite that cuts through summer's humidity — sliced thin, they dissolve into cold sōmen or scatter across chilled tofu like pink-tinged shards of clarity. Their fleeting season marks the pivot from crushing heat toward the first whisper of autumn cool.
my-ga-ginger-shoots.peak: High summer into early autumn, when the pale buds push through damp shade

my-ga-myoga-ginger.note: The pale pink buds of this shade-loving ginger offer a clean, resinous bite that cuts through humidity-dulled appetites — sliced thin, they float in chilled sōmen broth or crown a block of cold tofu. Myōga appears just as the body craves sharpness, a kitchen staple from the first cicadas through the lingering warmth of early September.
my-ga-myoga-ginger.peak: Early summer through early autumn, when heat demands bright astringency

my-ga-shoots.note: These blanched young stems of the myōga ginger plant emerge before the familiar flower buds, offering a milder, more delicate bite — crisp as celery, faintly perfumed, often sliced thin for clear soups or dressed simply with miso. They mark the brief window when ginger fields are thinned, a fleeting harvest known mainly to farmers and those who seek spring's quieter flavors.
my-ga-shoots.peak: Late spring through early summer, when the pale stalks push through warming soil

myoga-ginger.note: The pale pink buds emerge from shaded soil with a clean, resinous bite that cuts through summer's heaviness — sliced fine into cold sōmen or scattered over chilled tofu. Its sharp fragrance is said to clear the mind, a small mercy in the drowsy heat before the equinox.
myoga-ginger.peak: High summer through early autumn, when humidity hangs thick and appetites falter

nashi-asian-pear.note: Unlike its Western cousin, the nashi yields a spray of cold, granular juice the moment teeth break skin — more refreshing than sweet, like biting into autumn itself. It arrives as Obon lanterns are packed away, a crisp counterpoint to the lingering humidity, often peeled and quartered as a gesture of welcome to guests.
nashi-asian-pear.peak: Late summer into autumn, when the cicadas' drone gives way to cricket song

nasu-early-eggplant.note: The season's first eggplants arrive with thin, delicate skins and flesh so fine it barely resists the tooth — nothing like the dense globes of late summer. Grilled over charcoal until the skin blisters and collapses, or simmered in dashi until silken, early nasu marks the kitchen's pivot from spring's green austerity toward summer's abundance.
nasu-early-eggplant.peak: Early summer, when the first fruits appear slender and tender before the heat deepens

nasu-eggplant.note: The skin turns glossy purple-black, stretched taut over cream-colored flesh that collapses into silk when grilled over charcoal. Summer nasu are prized for their moisture and mild bitterness, while autumn nasu—sweetened by temperature swings—appear in miso-glazed dengaku and simmered dishes as the kitchen shifts toward warming preparations.
nasu-eggplant.peak: Late summer through early autumn, when the flesh grows dense and sweet after cool nights

natsu-mikan-summer-citrus.note: A thick-skinned citrus with segments that pull apart in uneven petals, its juice bracingly acidic with a faint honeyed finish that arrives only after months of patience on the branch. Once a Meiji-era novelty from Yamaguchi, it bridges the gap between winter's last satsuma and summer's first peach, its pale flesh a refreshment for the humid days ahead.
natsu-mikan-summer-citrus.peak: Late spring through early summer, when the bitter pith mellows and the flesh turns from sour to sweet-tart

new-garlic.note: Harvested young, new garlic offers a mild sweetness and moisture absent from cured heads — the cloves almost creamy when roasted whole, without the sharp bite that builds through storage. It arrives as rice-planting season begins, a brief window before summer's heat demands the familiar dried bulbs that will last through winter.
new-garlic.peak: Late spring to early summer, when the bulbs are lifted before their papery skins fully form

new-ginger.note: Pale as winter moonlight with tips blushed pink, new ginger arrives with flesh so delicate and fibers so fine it can be sliced tissue-thin and eaten raw, its heat bright but fleeting on the tongue. Pickled in sweet vinegar to a translucent coral, it becomes gari — the palate-cleanser that punctuates sushi meals through the humid months ahead.
new-ginger.peak: Early summer through midsummer, when the first tender rhizomes are lifted

new-potatoes.note: Harvested before their skins have set, new potatoes possess a waxy, almost translucent flesh and a sweetness that dissipates within days of digging. In Japanese kitchens, they are simmered whole in nikujaga or simply steamed and dressed with butter and a whisper of salt — a fleeting pleasure before the starchy storage varieties of autumn.
new-potatoes.peak: Late spring through early summer, when soil still holds the coolness of recent rains

nijisseiki-pear-20th-century-pear.note: A thin-skinned pear with jade-pale flesh so crisp it shatters between the teeth, releasing a flood of juice sweet as spring water. Developed in Chiba in 1888 and named for the century it would come to define, it remains the taste of early September — eaten chilled from the refrigerator while summer's heat still lingers in the afternoon.
nijisseiki-pear-20th-century-pear.peak: Early autumn, when the first cool nights arrive

okra.note: Cut crosswise, each pod reveals a perfect five-pointed star, its mucilaginous threads binding dashi and soy into something cool and slippery against the August heat. Though African in origin, okra has become inseparable from Japanese summer tables—blanched and dressed with katsuobushi, or simmered until it practically dissolves into curry, marking the days when even vegetables must work to refresh.
okra.peak: High summer, when cicadas reach their deafening chorus

pacific-saury-sanma.note: A slender, steel-blue fish whose rich flesh turns sweet and oily in September, best eaten simply salted and grilled until the skin blisters and the fat sizzles onto the coals below. The name itself — 'autumn sword fish' — marks it as the blade that cuts the season open, its smoke drifting through neighborhood streets as surely as the first cool evenings.
pacific-saury-sanma.peak: Early to mid-autumn, when the fish fatten before their southward migration

passion-fruit.note: Cut crosswise, the wrinkled purple shell reveals a glistening cavity of black seeds suspended in translucent golden pulp — intensely aromatic, at once tart and honeyed, with a fragrance that fills the room. Cultivated in Okinawa and Kagoshima, it arrives as a taste of the tropics during the humid months when mainland Japan craves bright, cooling flavors.
passion-fruit.peak: Early summer through late August, when subtropical vines heavy with fruit signal the height of southern warmth

pike-conger.note: A serpentine eel with a jaw full of fine bones, requiring the hamo-giri knife technique — hundreds of precise cuts that transform danger into silk, the flesh blooming white when blanched and dressed with tart umeboshi. Essential to Kyoto's summer kaiseki, it arrives from the Seto Inland Sea just as the city prepares for its great festival, proof that refinement can be carved from difficulty.
pike-conger.peak: Early summer through Gion Festival, when Kyoto's heat demands cooling elegance

pione-grape.note: A cross between Kyoho and Cannon Hall Muscat, Pione yields berries the size of small plums with blue-black skin that slips away to reveal translucent flesh of startling sweetness and faint musk. Its arrival marks the season when fruit shops arrange grapes like jewels in wooden boxes, gifts exchanged as summer's heat begins its slow retreat.
pione-grape.peak: Late summer through early autumn, when cicada cries give way to cricket song

pione-grapes.note: A cross between Kyoho and Cannon Hall Muscat, Pione grapes carry the deep purple-black bloom of their parent with flesh that slips cleanly from the skin, each orb bursting with concentrated sweetness balanced by faint acidity. They arrive as Obon fades and autumn approaches, their substantial clusters wrapped in paper and nested in wooden boxes — gifts that speak of late-summer abundance before the persimmons take their turn.
pione-grapes.peak: Late summer through early autumn, when the heat begins to relent

plum.note: These Western-style plums arrive with flesh that yields to the tooth in a single clean give, their skins taut and blushed from deep garnet to pale gold, each variety balancing tart snap against honeyed sweetness. They fill the gap between the preserved-ume season and the arrival of late summer stone fruits, eaten cold from the refrigerator as afternoon refreshment.
plum.peak: Early to midsummer, when the rains give way to pressing heat

prune-plum.note: These oval European plums arrive with flesh that yields to honey-sweetness, their skins carrying that particular dusty bloom that rubs away under the thumb. In Japan they appear briefly at fruit counters when summer tips toward autumn, eaten fresh or dried into the dense, wrinkled preserves that concentrate the season's last warmth.
prune-plum.peak: Late summer through early autumn, as the cicadas quiet

rakkyo-japanese-scallions.note: These small, ivory bulbs — somewhere between shallot and garlic in pungency — are harvested just as humidity settles over the archipelago, their crisp bite a natural foil for rich summer dishes. Pickled in sweet vinegar, they become the bright, crunchy accompaniment to Japanese curry, a pairing so fixed in the national palate that summer curry feels incomplete without their sharp punctuation.
rakkyo-japanese-scallions.peak: Early summer, when the plum rains begin their soft descent

rakkyo-scallion-bulbs.note: Small, ivory bulbs with a sharp bite somewhere between shallot and garlic, harvested before the humidity settles in. Pickled in sweet vinegar, they become the bright, crunchy counterpoint to rich summer curries — a preserve that carries the edge of June through the sweltering months ahead.
rakkyo-scallion-bulbs.peak: Early summer, when the tsuyu rains draw near

sake-salmon.note: Wild salmon arriving in autumn carry the deep coral flesh and clean fat of fish that have journeyed thousands of miles to spawn. Their return marks the start of preservation season — salted, dried, or cured as shiozake to sustain households through winter.
sake-salmon.peak: Autumn, when rivers run cold and fish return from the sea

sakuranbo-cherries.note: These are not the ornamental cherries of hanami but eating varieties—Satonishiki with their heart-shaped bodies yielding flesh that snaps clean and sweet against the teeth. They arrive in lacquered boxes as summer gifts, their season so brief that each fruit carries the weight of anticipation finally released.
sakuranbo-cherries.peak: Early summer, when the rains have not yet arrived and Yamagata orchards flush crimson

sakuranbo-early-cherries.note: These first cherries arrive small and taut-skinned, their flesh snapping with a brightness that leans more toward tartness than the honeyed depth of later harvests. They mark the threshold between spring's blossoms and summer's abundance — a fleeting sweetness eaten standing at the kitchen counter, stems still attached.
sakuranbo-early-cherries.peak: Early summer, when the plum rains have yet to settle in

sanma-pacific-saury.note: A slender, silver-blue fish whose belly fat reaches its richest point as September nights grow crisp — grilled whole over charcoal until the skin blisters and crackles, eaten with a squeeze of sudachi and grated daikon to cut the oils. The kanji themselves tell the story: 'autumn sword fish,' a blade of the season laid across the plate.
sanma-pacific-saury.peak: Early autumn, when the first cool winds carry the scent of charcoal smoke

sansai-mountain-vegetables.appearance: Varied forms of tender shoots, curled fronds, and pale buds still carrying traces of forest floor
sansai-mountain-vegetables.note: A collective term for wild edibles foraged from mountain and woodland — fiddlehead ferns, butterbur buds, fatsia shoots — each carrying its own bright bitterness that wakes the palate from winter's heaviness. Their brief appearance marks the threshold of the year's warmth, a tradition of seeking sustenance where cultivation cannot reach.
sansai-mountain-vegetables.peak: Early spring, when snowmelt reveals the first shoots on forested slopes
sansai-mountain-vegetables.serving_suggestion: Blanched and dressed simply with sesame or walnut, tempura-fried to temper their wild astringency, or simmered briefly in dashi

sansh-young-pepper-leaves.note: These young leaves carry a bright, almost electric tingle on the tongue, with a citrus-pine fragrance that cuts through rich dishes like simmered bamboo shoot or grilled eel. In the old calendar, sanshō marks the moment when winter's heaviness lifts — a green spark announcing the kitchen's turn toward clarity.
sansh-young-pepper-leaves.peak: Late spring, when the first tender leaves unfurl before the tree flowers

sardine-iwashi.note: The flesh turns richly oiled as waters warm, each small silver body firm enough to eat as sashimi yet soft enough to dissolve into tsumire fish cakes. Fishermen's wives once grilled them simply over charcoal at dawn — now that same sweet, mineral taste marks the shift from cherry blossoms to the drowsy heat of rainy season.
sardine-iwashi.peak: Late spring through early summer, when schools run thick along Pacific currents

satoimo-taro-root.note: These small, hairy corms yield flesh so slippery it seems to refuse the chopsticks — a quality called nameraka, prized in simmered dishes where the silken texture absorbs dashi to its core. Satoimo appears on the autumn moon-viewing altar beside susuki grass, marking the harvest moon when families once gave thanks for the tuber that sustained villages through lean winters.
satoimo-taro-root.peak: Mid-autumn through early winter, when the first frosts sweeten the flesh

sawara-spanish-mackerel.note: A long, silver-blue predator whose flesh turns from pale coral to creamy white when salted overnight and grilled until the skin blisters and chars at the edges, releasing oils that taste of the sea's own sweetness. The kanji itself tells the story—魚 beside 春—for this is the fish that announces spring's arrival in the Seto Inland Sea, though winter sawara from Sagami Bay, fattened by cold currents, offers a richness that rivals any toro.
sawara-spanish-mackerel.peak: Late spring, when wisteria drapes the arbors and the fish swim close to shore to spawn

sayori-halfbeak.note: A slender, silver-blue fish whose translucent flesh carries the faintest sweetness, prized for sashimi that gleams like morning light on still water. Its arrival signals the turn toward spring, served simply to honor the delicate clarity that cold seas impart before warmth softens the catch.
sayori-halfbeak.peak: Late winter through spring, when waters remain cold and flesh stays firm

sea-bass.note: A sleek predator with firm, translucent flesh that carries a clean sweetness, prized now for arai — ice-chilled sashimi slices that tighten into a texture both yielding and crisp. The fish grows through summer alongside the intensifying heat, its name changing as it matures, marking time like the cicadas that sing when it reaches peak flavor.
sea-bass.peak: High summer, when the fish chase baitfish into river mouths

shiira-mahi-mahi.note: A muscular, iridescent fish whose firm white flesh takes well to the grill, yielding a clean sweetness with none of the heaviness of fattier catches. In fishing towns along the Sea of Japan, its arrival signals the waning of summer heat, and it appears in home kitchens simply salt-grilled or simmered in soy and ginger before the autumn festivals begin.
shiira-mahi-mahi.peak: Late summer into early autumn, when the fish follow warm currents close to shore

shijimi-freshwater-clams.note: These small, dark-shelled clams yield a broth of surprising depth — faintly sweet, touched with iron, the color of weak tea. A bowl of shijimi miso soup after a night of drinking is less remedy than ritual, the liver's quiet ally as humidity settles over the archipelago.
shijimi-freshwater-clams.peak: Late spring through summer, when warm waters draw them toward the shallows

shimeji-mushroom.note: These tight clusters of slender stems and small brown caps carry a faint bitterness that sweetens only with heat, releasing an umami depth prized in nabemono and takikomi gohan. In the old calendar, their emergence marks the shift toward warming dishes, a quiet signal that the kitchen turns inward.
shimeji-mushroom.peak: Early autumn, as the first cool nights draw moisture through forest litter

shimeji-mushrooms.note: These clustered mushrooms grow in tight bundles, their small buff-colored caps firm and slightly bitter when raw, turning silken and faintly nutty once heat unlocks their umami. The Japanese saying 'smell matsutake, taste shimeji' speaks to their quiet supremacy in the autumn kitchen, where they slip into nabemono and takikomi gohan as the nights lengthen.
shimeji-mushrooms.peak: Mid-autumn, when cool rains settle into the forest floor

shine-muscat-grape.note: A seedless grape with skin so thin it yields without resistance, releasing flesh that tastes of muscat perfume and white honey. Developed in Japan and now the most coveted gift fruit of early autumn, each translucent green orb arrives when the harvest moon approaches and the season turns toward giving thanks.
shine-muscat-grape.peak: Late summer through early autumn, when the nights begin to cool

shine-muscat-grapes.note: A seedless grape with skin so thin you eat it whole, each orb bursting with a honeyed sweetness that carries faint notes of muscat and citrus blossom. Arriving as summer's heat loosens its grip, these grapes have become the new jewel of autumn gift-giving, their pale jade clusters wrapped in tissue like small treasures.
shine-muscat-grapes.peak: Late summer through early autumn, when the nights begin to cool

shirauo-icefish.note: These slender, glass-clear fish arrive when winter loosens its grip — their flesh so translucent you can see the dark thread of their spines. Eaten raw and still quivering in odorigui style, or barely poached in clear dashi, shirauo mark the threshold between cold and warmth, a fleeting delicacy that vanishes as quickly as plum blossoms scatter.
shirauo-icefish.peak: Early spring, as river mouths warm with snowmelt

shishit-shishito-pepper.note: Thin-skinned and mostly mild, these wrinkled fingers of pepper blister quickly in a hot pan, their flesh collapsing into something sweet and faintly smoky — though one in ten carries an unexpected bite of heat that keeps the eater alert. They arrive with the season of cold beer and summer festivals, charred at yatai stalls and served with nothing more than coarse salt and a squeeze of sudachi.
shishit-shishito-pepper.peak: Early summer through late summer, when humid heat coaxes them from the vine

shishito-pepper.note: Named for the wrinkled tip that resembles a lion's head, these thin-walled peppers blister quickly in hot oil, collapsing into tender pockets of grassy sweetness with an occasional surprising bite of heat — perhaps one in ten carries real fire. They arrive alongside the cicadas and cold beer of midsummer, charred whole and finished with nothing more than coarse salt and a squeeze of sudachi.
shishito-pepper.peak: Early summer through late August, when humid heat coaxes out their sweetest flesh

shiso.note: The deeply serrated leaves release a bright, almost electric fragrance when torn — part basil, part mint, part something entirely its own, cutting through the richness of raw fish or fried foods. In summer's sweltering kitchen, a few leaves wrapped around a bite of sashimi or tucked into somen bring a coolness that feels less like flavor than like breath.
shiso.peak: Early summer through the humid months, when the leaves grow lush before flowering

shiso-leaves.note: These jagged, aromatic leaves carry a flavor somewhere between mint and basil, with a faint citrus edge that cuts through the heaviness of rich foods. In summer's heat, a single shiso leaf wrapped around a bite of sashimi or tucked into a rice ball brings a coolness that feels almost medicinal — the plant has been used for centuries to settle the stomach and lift the spirits.
shiso-leaves.peak: Early summer through the humid months, when the leaves grow most fragrant

shiso-perilla.note: Each leaf carries a bright, almost mentholated sharpness that cuts through the humidity of rainy season—wrap one around a bite of sashimi and the fish tastes cleaner, cooler. Green shiso appears with the first summer cucumbers; by autumn, the plant offers its flower spikes for pickling and its seeds for crunching into miso.
shiso-perilla.peak: Early summer through the humid height of tsuyu, when leaves grow lush before flowering

shiso-perilla-leaves.note: Each leaf carries a sharp, almost medicinal brightness—part mint, part basil, part something wilder—that cuts through the humidity of summer meals, wrapped around sashimi or torn into cold somen. The red variety colors umeboshi in June's pickling season, while green shiso appears beside every raw fish offering, a quiet signal that the kitchen is awake to the season.
shiso-perilla-leaves.peak: Early summer through the lingering heat, when leaves grow broad and fragrant

silk-pod-peas.note: These flat, edible-podded peas earn their name from the silken sheen of their pale green skin, so thin it seems to hold light. Blanched for mere seconds and scattered over chirashi-zushi or floated in clear soup, they mark the fleeting weeks when spring still carries a whisper of coolness.
silk-pod-peas.peak: Late spring, as warm rains coax the vines into tender abundance

soramame-fava-beans.note: Named 'sky beans' for their upward-reaching pods, soramame are best eaten the day they're picked, when their jade-green flesh holds a grassy sweetness that fades within hours. Grilled whole in their woolly pods or simmered simply with salt, they mark the brief window between cherry blossoms and the plum rains.
soramame-fava-beans.peak: Late spring, as pods swell skyward in the warmth before tsuyu rains

spring-cabbage.note: Unlike the tight, pale heads of winter, spring cabbage arrives with leaves so tender they tear like wet paper, their sweetness bright enough to eat raw with nothing but a drift of salt. It marks the season when pickles lighten and salads return to the Japanese table, often simply shredded beside tonkatsu or wilted quickly in miso soup.
spring-cabbage.peak: Early spring through late April, when leaves are still loosely furled

spring-cabbage-haru-kyabetsu.note: Looser-headed than winter varieties, with pale yellow-green leaves so tender they're eaten raw in ribbons alongside tonkatsu, their sweetness bright and almost grassy. The arrival of spring cabbage signals the kitchen's turn toward lighter preparations—quick salt-pickles, fresh salads—as heavy braises give way to the gentler appetite of warming days.
spring-cabbage-haru-kyabetsu.peak: Early to mid-spring, when warming soil loosens the leaves' tight grip

squid.note: The flesh of summer squid is firm yet yielding, its sweetness clean as sea spray, best shown in sashimi cut so thin light passes through. From festival stalls sizzling with grilled surume to the delicate somen-ika of Hakodate, squid marks the passage from humid梅雨 into the bright appetite of summer.
squid.peak: Early summer through autumn, when waters warm along the Japan Sea coast

strawberries.note: Japanese strawberries are bred for delicate sweetness and tender flesh, varieties like Amaou and Tochiotome prized for their fragrance and jewel-like appearance on white porcelain. They mark the season between setsubun and hanami, filling department store displays and appearing in daifuku mochi while the last cold lingers.
strawberries.peak: Late winter through spring, when greenhouse-grown berries reach their sweetest intensity

strawberries-ichigo.note: Japanese strawberries are bred for sweetness over tartness, their flesh so tender it bruises at a careless touch — varieties like Amaou and Tochiotome yield berries with a perfumed intensity that fills the room when sliced. Though available nearly year-round now, their presence on winter tables and in spring wagashi marks the slow turn toward lighter days.
strawberries-ichigo.peak: Late winter through spring, when greenhouse cultivation meets rising warmth

sudachi.note: A small citrus no larger than a golf ball, prized not for eating whole but for its intensely aromatic juice — a few drops over grilled sanma or matsutake bring the umami into sudden, bright focus. Its season arrives just as the heat begins to soften, announcing the shift toward autumn's deeper flavors.
sudachi.peak: Late summer through early autumn, when the green rind still holds its sharp perfume

sudachi-citrus.note: A small citrus no larger than a golf ball, prized not for its flesh but for its intensely aromatic rind and bracingly sour juice — a few drops transform grilled sanma or matsutake soup with bright, clean acidity. Native to Tokushima, it arrives precisely when the autumn appetite returns, cutting through the richness of the season's first fatty fish.
sudachi-citrus.peak: Late summer through early autumn, when the green rind holds its sharpest perfume

suika-early-watermelon.note: These early specimens arrive smaller and denser than their midsummer cousins, their flesh a concentrated pink with a crispness that yields cleanly to the teeth. They mark the threshold of true summer, appearing on tables just as families begin thinking of fireworks and the sound of wind chimes.
suika-early-watermelon.peak: Early summer, when the first humid nights settle over the lowlands

suika-first-watermelons.note: The season's first watermelons arrive with flesh still pale at the edges, their sweetness restrained and clean — a coolness you taste before you feel. Split open at riverbanks and summer festivals, suika marks the threshold into the long days of heat, its black seeds scattered like the nights growing shorter.
suika-first-watermelons.peak: Early summer, as the rains give way to the first true heat

suika-watermelon.note: The flesh should give way with an audible crack when split, its sweetness concentrated where the seeds cluster darkest near the rind. Chilled in well water or a mountain stream, then eaten on the engawa as evening cools, suika marks the brief window when summer's intensity is not yet burden but pure gift.
suika-watermelon.peak: High summer, from the lesser heat through the great heat when cicadas reach full cry

summer-daikon.note: Unlike the mild, sweet daikon of winter, summer daikon carries a peppery sting that cuts through humid days — grated raw, it becomes a cooling condiment with real presence. It arrives when cooks need something bracing to wake the palate, a counterpoint to the season's heavier flavors.
summer-daikon.peak: Early summer through late August, when heat draws out its sharp bite

sumomo-japanese-plum.note: Smaller and rounder than its Western cousins, the sumomo offers flesh that ranges from honey-gold to deep crimson, with a tartness at the skin that yields to syrupy sweetness near the stone. Its arrival marks the true beginning of summer's fruit abundance, often preserved in rock sugar to make a cooling cordial drunk through the long August heat.
sumomo-japanese-plum.peak: Early to midsummer, as the humid air settles after the plum rains

suzuki-japanese-sea-bass.note: A fish that grows into its name — called different things at different sizes, finally earning 'suzuki' only when its flesh turns firm and clean, with a sweetness that takes well to a brief sear or thin-sliced as sashimi. Summer suzuki, pulled from warm shallows, marks the season when fishermen work through humid nights and morning markets smell of brine and ice.
suzuki-japanese-sea-bass.peak: Early summer through August, when heat settles over coastal waters

suzuki-sea-bass.note: A fish that changes names as it grows — seigo, fukko, then finally suzuki — its flesh at summer peak is clean and sweet, firm enough to hold its shape in usuzukuri slices yet yielding a delicate fat that blooms on the tongue. The character for suzuki contains the radical for 'age' and 'fish' together, honoring how the Japanese palate has long prized this bass at its most mature, served as arai washed in ice water to tighten the meat into something bracingly alive.
suzuki-sea-bass.peak: Early summer through the height of the rainy season, when waters warm and the fish fatten

sweet-corn.note: Harvested at dawn and rushed to market, the kernels still hold their milk-sweet juice — bite through the taut skin and the sugars haven't yet begun their slow turn to starch. In Japan, corn appears grilled at festival stalls brushed with soy and mirin, its charred edges carrying the smoke of summer nights.
sweet-corn.peak: High summer, when cicadas reach their full chorus

sweet-potato-satsumaimo.note: Freshly dug sweet potatoes need weeks of curing before their dense, chestnut-like flesh develops the honeyed sweetness that caramelizes at the edges of a stone-roasted imo. The yaki-imo vendor's whistle through cold evening streets marks the true arrival of winter's comfort.
sweet-potato-satsumaimo.peak: Late autumn through early winter, when starches have slowly converted to sugars in storage

sweetfish.note: A slender, elegant river fish whose flesh carries the faint fragrance of watermelon and fresh cucumber — the scent of the algae it grazes from sun-warmed stones. Grilled whole over charcoal with a crust of coarse salt, its arrival marks the true beginning of summer, when fishing boats appear on mountain streams and the air grows heavy with approaching rain.
sweetfish.peak: Early summer through the height of the rainy season, when rivers run cold and clear

sweetfish-ayu.note: A slender river fish whose flesh carries the faint fragrance of watermelon and fresh cucumber — the scent of clean mountain streams translated into protein. Grilled whole on skewers over charcoal, its bitter entrails prized as much as its sweet meat, ayu marks the true arrival of summer and the opening of cormorant fishing season along ancient rivers like the Nagara.
sweetfish-ayu.peak: Early summer through midsummer, when rivers run cool beneath the June rains

t-gan-winter-melon.note: Despite its name suggesting winter, this pale gourd reaches its prime in July and August, its translucent flesh turning almost glass-like when simmered in dashi, cooling the body from within. The name speaks to its remarkable keeping quality — harvested in summer's blaze, it waits patiently in the pantry until the first frosts, a bridge between seasons stored in a single rind.
t-gan-winter-melon.peak: High summer, when cicadas drone through the humid afternoons

tai-sea-bream.note: The firm, translucent flesh carries a clean sweetness that intensifies as spawning season approaches, the skin crisping to a burnished rose when salt-grilled. Called 'king of fish' and essential to celebrations from New Year to weddings, its very name echoes 'medetai' — auspicious — making it inseparable from moments of joy in the Japanese calendar.
tai-sea-bream.peak: Late spring through early summer, when cherry blossoms scatter and waters warm

takenoko-bamboo-shoots.note: Freshly dug shoots, still pale and faintly sweet, must be boiled within hours before bitterness sets in—the flesh should yield like young daikon, with a clean vegetal snap. Their arrival marks the brief window when earth is soft enough to harvest them before they breach the surface and toughen in sunlight.
takenoko-bamboo-shoots.peak: Mid-spring, during kokuu when grain rains soften the soil

tako-octopus.note: Summer tako yields firm, resilient flesh with a clean sweetness that snaps between the teeth — boiled just until the skin turns that distinctive burgundy, sliced thin for sunomono or simmered tender in oden. The fishermen of Akashi have prized these waters for centuries, timing their catch to the strong Seto Inland Sea currents that give the octopus its prized texture.
tako-octopus.peak: Summer through early autumn, when the creature fattens in warm coastal waters

tomato.note: At peak ripeness, the flesh gives way to a balance of sweetness and faint acidity, the skin still warm from the afternoon heat. Though a relatively recent arrival to Japanese tables, summer tomatoes now anchor the kitchen's brief window of raw abundance—sliced simply with salt, or crushed into chilled hiyashi chūka noodles.
tomato.peak: High summer, when the sun draws sugars up through the vine

tomorokoshi-corn.note: Freshly harvested ears possess a milky sweetness that fades within hours of picking, the kernels so tender they burst against the teeth with grassy, almost floral notes. Grilled over charcoal and brushed with soy, it becomes the taste of Obon evenings and summer matsuri, eaten standing in the blue smoke of festival stalls.
tomorokoshi-corn.peak: High summer, when cicadas reach their fullest chorus

tomorokoshi-young-corn.note: Harvested before the kernels fully set, young corn offers a milky sweetness and tender cob you can eat whole — the silk still pale, the husk tight with morning dew. It arrives with the first cicadas, grilled over charcoal at summer festivals or simmered briefly in salted water, a fleeting taste before the ears grow starchy and robust.
tomorokoshi-young-corn.peak: Early summer, from the solstice through the height of the rainy season

tsuru-murasaki-malabar-spinach.note: A climbing vine whose thick, glossy leaves release a gentle mucilage when cooked, lending a cooling slip to summer dishes that cuts through the season's heaviness. It thrives precisely when true spinach cannot, filling the gap in the kitchen between the last spring greens and autumn's return.
tsuru-murasaki-malabar-spinach.peak: High summer, when the heat brings its vines to fullest vigor

tsurumurasaki-malabar-spinach.note: A climbing vine whose heart-shaped leaves release a subtle mucilage when cut, lending body to clear soups and a cooling slickness against the August heat. Its deep green arrives just as true spinach has long since bolted, offering the Japanese summer kitchen a heat-loving stand-in with an earthier, slightly mineral edge.
tsurumurasaki-malabar-spinach.peak: High summer, when the cicadas reach their fever pitch

udo-mountain-asparagus.note: A tall, celery-pale stalk with a flavor caught between asparagus and fennel, prized for its crisp bite and faint bitterness that speaks of wild places. Blanched and dressed in vinegared miso or sliced raw into salads, udo marks the brief window when foragers climb still-cold hillsides to harvest what cannot be rushed or cultivated into mildness.
udo-mountain-asparagus.peak: Early spring, as snow recedes from mountain slopes

ume-green-plum.note: Hard, intensely sour, and fragrant with a sharp green perfume, these unripe plums are never eaten raw but transformed through salt or sugar into umeboshi and umeshu. Their arrival marks the start of tsuyu season and sets households to their annual ritual of preserving — glass jars lined up on kitchen counters, catching the grey light.
ume-green-plum.peak: Early summer, as the plum rains begin their soft descent

ume-green-plums.note: Hard, astringent, and intensely fragrant, green plums arrive too sour to eat raw — their flesh meant instead for transformation into umeshu liqueur or the salt-preserved umeboshi that will sustain appetites through humid months ahead. The arrival of aoume signals the start of tsuyu, the plum rains, and sets kitchens across Japan into a quiet rhythm of sterilizing jars and weighing rock sugar.
ume-green-plums.peak: Early summer, as the rainy season approaches and humidity thickens the air

ume-green-plums-just-appearing.note: Hard, astringent, and intensely fragrant, green plums arrive too sour to eat raw — their sharp vegetal scent fills the kitchen as they wait to be transformed into umeshu or umeboshi. Their appearance marks the start of tsuyu, the plum rains, when patient cooks begin the slow alchemy of salt and time.
ume-green-plums-just-appearing.peak: Early summer, as the rainy season approaches

wakame-young-seaweed.note: Freshly harvested wakame has a silken texture and bright mineral sweetness that fades within hours of leaving the sea — nothing like its dried counterpart. It arrives in markets just as miso soup shifts from winter's root vegetables to spring's delicate greens, the seaweed's tender fronds signaling the ocean's own turning of the season.
wakame-young-seaweed.peak: Early spring, when cold currents still run along the coast

water-spinach.note: Named for its hollow stems that stay crisp even after a flash in the wok, this Southeast Asian green thrives in Japan's muggy July and August, offering a texture between spinach and morning glory vine. It arrived relatively recently but has earned its place in the summer kitchen, stir-fried with garlic and a splash of oyster sauce when heavier greens wilt in the heat.
water-spinach.peak: High summer, when the stems grow fastest in the humid heat

watermelon.note: The flesh should give way with an audible crack when split, its sweetness concentrated in the pale heart where seeds cluster darkest. At Obon, chilled wedges appear on verandas after the evening bath, the rind later floated in rivers as lanterns to guide ancestral spirits home.
watermelon.peak: High summer, when cicadas reach full chorus and the heat settles into the bones

white-peach.note: Japanese white peaches yield to the slightest pressure, their pale flesh so juicy it must be eaten over the sink, fragrant with a sweetness that seems to hold the whole of summer afternoons. They arrive at Obon season, offered at family altars and shared as gifts, their brief perfection a reminder that the most fleeting things deserve the most care.
white-peach.peak: High summer, from late July through August when the heat draws out the sugars

white-peach-hakut.note: Cradled in foam nets at fruit shops, these pale beauties yield flesh so tender it bruises at a glance, their perfume filling a room before the first bite releases floods of honeyed juice. The white peach arrives as a cooling grace note in the humid peak of summer, given as elegant gifts in paulownia boxes or eaten chilled over the sink, juice running down wrists.
white-peach-hakut.peak: High summer, from late July through August, when the cicadas reach their crescendo

yellow-plums.note: These are ume left on the branch until they blush gold and yield to gentle pressure, their flesh now fragrant with apricot-like sweetness rather than the sharp green astringency of earlier pickings. Arriving at the close of umeshigoto season, they are prized for making umeboshi with softer texture and mellower taste, or for jams that capture the last breath of early summer.
yellow-plums.peak: Late June, as tsuyu rains reach their deepest

yellowtail-amberjack.note: The winter buri, called kan-buri, carries ribbons of rich fat between its rosy flesh — each slice gleaming with an almost sweet unctuousness that coats the tongue. This is the fish of year-end celebrations, simmered in sweetened soy for osechi boxes or grilled with teriyaki glaze as families gather to close one year and welcome the next.
yellowtail-amberjack.peak: Deep winter, when cold currents fatten the flesh beneath silvery skin

yellowtail-amberjack-kanpachi.note: Named for the dark band between its eyes that forms the kanji for 'eight' (八), kanpachi yields flesh that is leaner and more delicate than its buri cousins — pale pink, with a clean sweetness and subtle crunch when sliced for sashimi. It arrives at the height of summer when heavier fish feel wrong, offering a lightness that suits the season's humid weight.
yellowtail-amberjack-kanpachi.peak: High summer through early autumn, when the fish fatten in warm currents
